findings.location: sections/homily/90-note.tex, References, the fifth entry: "St Augustine, \work{Enarrationes in Psalmos} 109, 3--6, Latin text of Migne, PL 37."
findings.problem: The entry cites the Latin as "Latin text of Migne, PL 37" without saying that it was read from a tracked digital transcription rather than from the printed columns. The reviewed expansive study's own apparatus discloses the delivery for this very source at sections/90-apparatus.tex line 114, "Latin text of Migne, PL 36--37 (Wikisource and Corpus Corporum)", and the leaf binds the passage to artifact.augustine.enarrationes-in-psalmos.latin-migne-corpus-corporum-wikisource-web-2026-09-05.wikisource-part-11-latin-text, which is where I verified the quoted matter ("Respondeamus omnino quod Judaei, sed non remaneamus ubi Judaei" and "in forma Dei ... ideo Dominus David: sed temetipsum exinanisti formam servi accipiens; inde filius David"). The same holds for the Jerome entry, whose passage record states in terms that printed-image collation was not performed. The note is otherwise scrupulous about routes, flagging the 1861 Cummiskey English as a historical study aid and not an approved liturgical translation, naming the NPNF translators for both Greek and Latin Fathers quoted in English, and saying that the Offertory antiphon is a compilation quoted in no English at all, so these two entries are the only place a reader could take a printed-page reading to have been performed when it was not.
findings.required_result: The References either name the delivery through which each Latin text was actually read, matching the disclosure the reviewed study's apparatus already carries for the Enarrationes, or the note's "English quoted, and its route" paragraph states once that the Latin of Augustine on Ps 109 and of Jerome on Daniel is read from tracked digital transcriptions of Migne and not from the printed columns.

summary: Reviewed the standalone homily for the Seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost (homily.tex with sections/homily/10-homily.tex and sections/homily/90-note.tex) as speech and as exegesis: the spoken body is continuous, speakable preaching with no editorial instruction, footnote dependence or inline citation, carrying one clear exegetical argument built on Chrysostom's join of the Gospel's two halves, so that the God of the great commandment is shown to be the Christ whose third question went unanswered, and closing on the Creed, the offering, Communion and the eternal remedy. Evidence was checked against primary text rather than against the research records: the Douay-Rheims of Mt 22:36, 37, 39, 42, 45, 46, Eph 4:2-6, Ps 118:137 and 124, and Ps 75:12 against the repository's indexed bible via tools/mass-propers; the 1861 Cummiskey Collect and Postcommunion against the leaf's collated propers/verified.md, together with the Missal pages 398-400, nos. 1602-1611 and the Creed rubric at no. 1607; and Augustine De doctrina christiana I.22.21, Chrysostom Homilies on Matthew 71 (three quotations), Augustine Enarrationes in Psalmos 109 and Jerome Commentarii in Danielem on 9:5 against the tracked retained artifacts in src/sources, all four verifying verbatim at the loci the note gives. The spoken body counts 1,429 words exactly as the note states, the pace arithmetic is correct and claims no timed delivery, the contested points the study records (the distribution of Eph 4:6, Daniel's own sin, the lawyer's motive) are each avoided or stated in a form both sides admit, and no anecdote, personal experience, clerical identity or composed prayer appears. Verdict: no blocking defect; one advisory on a source-route disclosure in the References. Limits: I did not collate printed page images, build or inspect the rendered PDF, or hear or time any delivery.
